summary: Specifies the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) data plane for MPLS networks. It reuses existing pseudowire encapsulations and MPLS Traffic Engineering mechanisms, building on the DetNet architecture and data plane framework to carry time-sensitive flows.

plainLanguage.summary: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) promises that some traffic arrives almost without loss and always within a known delay limit. This document explains how to carry such traffic over an MPLS network, the label-based network technology used by many carriers. It reuses the labels, reserved paths and traffic engineering that MPLS already provides.

subtitle: How Deterministic Networking flows are carried over an MPLS network, using a control word, a service label and forwarding labels.

tldr.problem: Some traffic must be delivered with extremely low packet loss and a bounded end-to-end delay, but ordinary IP networks give no such promise.
tldr.mechanism: The document reuses MPLS to build that promise. It adds a DetNet control word with a packet sequence number, a service label that names the flow, and forwarding labels that steer the packet along a reserved path.
tldr.outcome: A network that already runs MPLS can offer deterministic delivery by configuring labels and traffic engineering it already knows. The design also covers replication, duplicate removal and reordering for protection.

facts.label: Labels per packet
facts.value: One S-Label and zero or more F-Labels

facts.label: OAM indicator
facts.value: First nibble of the d-CW: 0x0 for data, 0x1 for OAM

today: RFC 8964 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it defines the MPLS data plane for DetNet on top of the DetNet architecture in RFC 8655 and the DetNet data plane framework in RFC 8938.

sections.title: Deterministic Networking over MPLS
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is a service a network can offer to DetNet flows. It delivers data flows with extremely low packet loss rates and bounded end-to-end delivery latency. The general background and concepts live in the DetNet architecture, RFC 8655.

This document specifies the data plane operation and the on-wire encapsulation of DetNet flows over an MPLS-based Packet Switched Network (PSN). It reuses the existing pseudowire encapsulations and the MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) mechanisms, so a network that already runs MPLS can add deterministic behaviour using labels and paths it already knows.

The types of traffic carried in DetNet, and the details of how MPLS-encapsulated DetNet is carried over each underlying network technology, are out of scope for this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic must arrive on time and almost never be lost. This document shows how to give that traffic a reserved lane across a network that uses MPLS labels.

sections.title: Two Sub-Layers of the DetNet Data Plane
sections.content:
The DetNet architecture splits the data plane functions into two sub-layers. The service sub-layer provides service functions such as protection and reordering, using the Packet Replication, Elimination and Ordering Functions (PREOF). The forwarding sub-layer provides forwarding assurance: low loss, assured latency and limited out-of-order delivery.

In the MPLS adaptation, the service sub-layer is carried by a DetNet control word (d-CW) and a service label (S-Label), at the bottom of the label stack. The forwarding sub-layer is carried by zero or more forwarding labels (F-Labels), at the top of the stack.

A node that receives a DetNet flow uses the local context associated with a received S-Label to decide which local operations to apply to that packet. S-Label values are driven by the receiver, not the sender, so a label identifies a flow only within the label space of the node that assigned it.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet splits the work in two. One part copies, removes and reorders packets to protect the flow. The other part reserves capacity and pins a path so the packets arrive on time. MPLS labels carry both parts.

sections.title: The DetNet MPLS Encapsulation
sections.content:
The encapsulation has four parts. A DetNet control word (d-CW) carries the sequencing information used for packet replication and duplicate elimination, and the indicator that separates operations traffic from user data. A service label (S-Label) identifies the DetNet flow at the receiving service sub-layer node. Zero or more forwarding labels (F-Labels) direct the packet along the Label Switched Path (LSP) to the next service sub-layer node. The necessary data-link encapsulation is then applied before transmission over the physical media.

The S-Label is similar to a pseudowire (PW) label. The LSP that carries the packet is not restricted to any particular way of being set up; MPLS-LDP, MPLS-TE, MPLS-TP and MPLS Segment Routing are all listed as possible. Because Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP) may be in use, the S-Label may be the only label received at the terminating DetNet service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet gets a small control word, one service label and, usually, forwarding labels. The service label says which flow the packet belongs to. The forwarding labels say where to send it.

sections.title: The DetNet Control Word
sections.content:
The d-CW conforms to the Generic PW MPLS Control Word (PWMCW) defined in RFC 4385. It is 32 bits long. Bits 0 to 3 must be set to zero. The remaining bits, 4 to 31, carry the DetNet sequence number, an unsigned value in a circular number space with no restriction on the initial value.

A node that adds the d-CW must keep a separate sequence number space for each DetNet application flow. Three field lengths must be supported: 0 bits, 16 bits and 28 bits. The length is provisioned on a per-DetNet-service basis by the controller plane. A 0-bit length means no DetNet sequence number is used for the flow, and the field must then be set to zero on all packets sent for that flow.

When the length is 16 or 28 bits, the sequence number must be incremented by one for each new application-flow packet sent. With a 16-bit length, d-CW bits 4 to 15 must be set to zero. The values carried in the field can wrap, and zero is an ordinary sequence number: with a 16-bit sequence the values run 65535, 0, 1. This differs from RFC 4448, where a sequence number of zero means the sequence number check algorithm is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The control word is 32 bits. Four bits are always zero and the rest carry a packet counter. The counter can be 16 or 28 bits wide, and it wraps around to zero and keeps going. Zero is a normal counter value here, not a signal to stop checking.

sections.title: Replication, Elimination and Ordering
sections.content:
Three functions carry out the work of the service sub-layer. Each is optional, and its use for a particular DetNet service must be provisioned by the controller plane.

The Packet Replication Function (PRF) sends the same application data over several outgoing DetNet member flows, each using its own forwarding sub-layer LSP. An S-Label value must be configured per outgoing member flow, and the same d-CW field value must be used on all outgoing member flows for each replicated packet.

The Packet Elimination Function (PEF) discards duplicate instances of a sequence number that the receiver has already seen. It must not be used with DetNet flows configured with a d-CW sequence number field length of 0 bits.

The Packet Ordering Function (POF) processes packets in the order indicated by the received d-CW sequence number, which may not be the order they arrived in. An implementation may require PEF and POF to be used together, and there is no requirement on the order of execution between them. A node may limit how many out-of-order packets it can process, because those buffers add to the latency of the flow.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can send each packet along two paths to survive a failure, throw away the copy that arrives second, and put the packets back in order if they arrive shuffled. Each of these three jobs is switched on separately for each flow.

sections.title: Forwarding Labels and the Forwarding Sub-Layer
sections.content:
F-Labels provide LSP-based connectivity between the nodes that run the service sub-layer. A node sending a DetNet flow pushes zero or more F-Labels on top of the S-Label, and the set of F-Labels to push is provisioned per outgoing S-Label. When several sets of F-Labels or outgoing interfaces are provisioned, a copy of the outgoing packet is made per set, and each copy receives its own F-Labels.

On receipt, the node identifies the DetNet service from the S-Label. When platform labels are used for S-Labels, the S-Label alone is enough. Otherwise the incoming F-Labels, and optionally the incoming interface, are used together with the S-Label to identify the service. Which of these a node uses is a local implementation choice.

F-Labels map to explicit routes and allocated resources, and the topmost outgoing F-Label must be associated with a provisioned outgoing interface and, for non-point-to-point interfaces, a next-hop LSR. Nodes must also defend the DetNet quality of service. Packets received that are not associated with a completed resource allocation must be discarded or remarked, a resource allocated for DetNet must never be used for a packet that does not match the corresponding flow, and a flow must not exceed its allocated resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding labels are the ordinary MPLS labels that carry a packet along a chosen path with reserved capacity. The node that receives a packet uses the service label to find which flow it belongs to, and the forwarding labels to work out where the packet came in.

sections.title: Class of Service and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Class of Service (CoS) and Quality of Service (QoS) are often used interchangeably, and this document keeps them apart. CoS refers to mechanisms that give traffic a forwarding treatment based on traffic classification that is not tied to a particular flow, such as the Differentiated Services code point in the IP header, the MPLS label Traffic Class field or the IEEE 802.1p priority code point. QoS refers to treatment based on flow-specific classification.

Beyond explicit routes and packet replication and elimination, DetNet provides zero congestion loss and bounded latency and jitter. A baseline set of QoS capabilities for DetNet flows carried in pseudowires and MPLS can be provided by MPLS-TE, and TE LSPs can support explicit routes for path pinning. The mechanisms that deliver the service include discrete resource allocation, admission control, flow identification and isolation, and sometimes path control, traffic protection, shaping, policing and remarking. Protocols that support this kind of control include RSVP and RSVP-TE.
sections.plainLanguage: Class of service treats all traffic in a class the same way. Quality of service promises a named flow its own reserved capacity and a limit on delay. DetNet needs the second kind.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security aspects unique to DetNet are those that protect the quality of service itself, since delivering data flows with extremely low packet loss rates and bounded end-to-end delivery latency may not be possible against an adversary who can arbitrarily drop or delay any or all traffic. This document considers a weaker attacker, one who does not control the physical links of the DetNet domain but may control a node inside it.

MPLS provides no native security services for confidentiality or integrity, and this document adds no application header information. Application flows can be protected through the underlying technology, for example with IPsec for IP flows or with MACsec for IP over Ethernet. To keep the service available, denial of service and delay attacks are met with existing mechanisms such as policing and shaping incoming traffic, authentication and authorization of network equipment, and monitoring of the delay on the LSP. If a delay attack is suspected, traffic may be moved to an alternate path by changing the LSP or the PREOF configuration.

Identifying DetNet flows on a per-flow basis at the management and control level gives a controller plane attacker more information about the data flows than a controller plane without per-flow identification would. The document calls this an inherent property of DetNet that should be weighed when deciding whether DetNet suits a given use case.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet promises tight delay bounds, and an attacker inside the network can break that promise. The document says so plainly, and points to ordinary protections: encrypt the traffic, police what comes in, and watch the delay on the path.

items.title: Service sub-layer
items.text: Protects the flow: copies packets onto member flows, removes duplicates and puts packets back in order.

items.title: Forwarding sub-layer
items.text: Delivers the flow: explicit routes, reserved resources, low loss and a bounded delay.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: The DetNet sequence number. The field is 28 bits, 16 bits (bits 4 to 15 set to zero) or 0 bits when the flow uses no sequence number.

items.title: PRF
items.text: Replication. Sends the same packet on several member flows, with the same control word value on each.

items.title: PEF
items.text: Elimination. Throws away copies of a sequence number that has already been received.

items.title: POF
items.text: Ordering. Delivers packets in sequence number order, not in arrival order.
